blocks.heading: Primary and secondary research
blocks.text: Primary research gathers new information for the current purpose, through surveys, interviews, observation or other direct collection. Secondary research uses information that already exists, such as previous sales records, published reports or earlier studies. Primary work can be tailored and current but costs time and can suffer sampling or question bias. Secondary information may be quicker and cheaper but may use an unsuitable market, date or definition. Internal/external is a different distinction: old business sales records are internal secondary data, while a newly commissioned customer survey is primary even though customers are outside the business. Assess relevance, accuracy, age and coverage rather than assuming either category is superior.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Meals compares a new survey of intended buyers with its existing sales records and a published regional report. The survey is primary. Existing records are internal secondary data and the report is external secondary data. The report’s regional scope may not describe Tula’s specific local buyers.

blocks.heading: Primary research
blocks.text: Primary research is the collection and collation of original data via direct contact with potential or existing customers. It is also called field research. Surveys, interviews and relevant observation can gather new evidence for a specified decision. The business controls the questions and focus but needs time, suitable sampling and unbiased collection. Paying another researcher to gather new data does not make it secondary.

blocks.text: Eha Bags commissions new interviews about a proposed bag. The information is primary because it is newly gathered for this purpose, even though an outside researcher collects it.

blocks.heading: Secondary research
blocks.text: Secondary research uses existing information rather than collecting new data for the present question. It is also called desk research. It can use internal records or external publications and may give an inexpensive starting point. Check the date, definitions, source reliability and relevance to the target market. Data collected for another purpose may leave the current question unanswered.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ota Foods examines last year’s sales records and an existing public report. Both are secondary sources. The sales records are internal and the report external, so secondary is not a synonym for outside the business.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the research classifications: Omi Meals uses old internal sales records and commissions new interviews with outside customers.

The existing records are secondary research and internal information. The new interviews are primary research even though respondents are outside the business. New/existing describes primary/secondary; inside/outside describes source location. These questions must be answered separately.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Research evidence and a research decision
blocks.text:
Tula Meals surveys forty intended local customers about format at a feasible price using neutral questions. Wrap receives 18 responses, box 12 and salad 10. It considers a small paid-sales trial before committing to a large launch. Historical records concern a different menu. For part (b) only, the forty respondents are now known to be the owner’s friends from outside the intended local market. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Tula’s proposed small trial using the original research. [12]
b Evaluate the research basis after the respondent information changes. Explain which parts of the conclusion should change or hold. [12]

a Local intended buyers and neutral questions provide a relevant starting point, but forty preferences do not establish actual orders. A bar chart can compare 18, 12 and 10; it cannot remove uncertainty. Prefer a small paid trial and review sales before scaling. b Friends outside the target market weaken representativeness despite unchanged counts and correct charts. Do not use the original preference lead to set the local offer confidently. Gather new evidence from suitable target buyers with neutral questions, then conduct a limited trial. The preference for caution holds, but the original evidence’s relevance no longer holds; redrawing the chart cannot repair the sample.
